title: Series LCR Circuit in Alternating Current
short_intro: A series LCR circuit consists of a resistor, an inductor, and a capacitor connected in series across an alternating voltage source. It exhibits electrical resonance at a specific frequency where the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel each other out.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic understanding of impedance, phase angle, resonant frequency, and maximum current condition in an AC series circuit containing R, L, and C components.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed analytical treatment of sharpness of resonance, Q-factor, half-power frequencies, band-width, and phasor diagram analysis with complex impedance.

prerequisites: Alternating current fundamentals (RMS and peak values)
Reactance of pure inductor and pure capacitor

concept_notes.heading: Impedance and Phasor Representation
bullets: The total opposition offered by a series LCR circuit to the flow of alternating current is called impedance (Z).
Impedance is represented as a complex number: Z = R + j(X_L - X_C), where X_L = omega L and X_C = 1/(omega C).
The magnitude of impedance is given by Z = sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}.

concept_notes.heading: Phase Angle and Power Factor
bullets: The phase angle (phi) between the alternating voltage and current is given by (\tanphi = (X_L - X_C) / R).
When X_L > X_C, the circuit is inductive, current lags voltage, and (phi) is positive.
When X_C > X_L, the circuit is capacitive, current leads voltage, and (phi) is negative.

concept_notes.heading: Electrical Resonance
bullets: Resonance occurs when the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance (X_L = X_C).
At resonance, the net reactance is zero, impedance is minimum (Z = R), and current is maximum.
The resonant angular frequency is (omega_0 = 1 / sqrt{LC}).

concept_notes.heading: Quality Factor and Sharpness of Resonance
bullets: The Quality factor (Q-factor) measures the sharpness of resonance and voltage magnification across L or C at resonance.
Q-factor is defined as the ratio of resonant frequency to bandwidth: Q = omega_0 / (Deltaomega) = (omega_0 L) / R = 1 / (omega_0 C R).
A higher Q-factor indicates a sharper resonance curve and a more selective circuit.

derivations.title: Impedance and Phase Angle of Series LCR Circuit
derivations.conditions: AC source E = E_0 sin(omega t) connected across series combination of R, L, and C.
steps: Let the alternating current in the circuit be represented by i = i_0 sin(omega t).
The potential difference across resistor R is V_R = i_0 R sin(omega t) (in phase with current).
The potential difference across inductor L is V_L = i_0 X_L sin(omega t + pi/2) (leading current by 90 degrees).
The potential difference across capacitor C is V_C = i_0 X_C sin(omega t - pi/2) (lagging current by 90 degrees).
Using phasor addition, the total voltage E_0 = sqrt{V_{R0}^2 + (V_{L0} - V_{C0})^2} = sqrt{(i_0 R)^2 + (i_0 X_L - i_0 X_C)^2}.
Expressing impedance as Z = E_0 / i_0, we obtain Z = sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}.
derivations.result: Z = sqrt{R^2 + (omega L - \frac{1}{omega C})^2} \text{ and } \tanphi = \frac{omega L - \frac{1}{omega C}}{R}

derivations.title: Resonant Frequency and Bandwidth
derivations.conditions: Condition for resonance X_L = X_C and half-power frequencies where power drops to half of maximum.
steps: Equate inductive and capacitive reactances: omega_0 L = 1 / (omega_0 C).
Solve for omega_0 to get omega_0^2 = 1 / (LC).
Define half-power frequencies (omega_1) and (omega_2) where current drops to (1/sqrt{2}) of maximum value, meaning impedance Z = (sqrt{2}R).
Set up the condition: (omega L - 1/(omega C) = pm R).
Solving the quadratic equations yields the frequency band limits, giving bandwidth (Deltaomega = omega_2 - omega_1 = R / L).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Current vs Frequency Resonance Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bell-shaped curve plotting RMS current (I_rms) on the y-axis against frequency (f) on the x-axis, showing peaks at f_0 for different values of resistance R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Smaller resistance values yield sharper peaks with higher maximum current, whereas larger resistance values flatten the resonance curve.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in conceptual questions regarding the effect of damping (resistance) on resonance sharpness.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Phasor Diagram of Series LCR Circuit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A vector diagram with current vector along the reference axis, V_R in phase, V_L leading by 90 degrees, and V_C lagging by 90 degrees.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates vector addition of voltages in an AC circuit to obtain total applied voltage vector.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to derive impedance formula and determine phase relationships.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Impedance vs Frequency Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A hyperbolic-parabolic curve showing individual reactances X_L (linear) and X_C (inverse), and total impedance Z having a minimum value equal to R at resonance frequency f_0.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visually displays how total impedance drops to its minimum resistive component at the resonant frequency.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Asked in matching and graphical identification questions in PGT physics exams.

solved_numericals.question: A 100 Omega resistor, a 0.5 H inductor, and a 10 mu F capacitor are connected in series across a 200 V, 50 Hz AC source. Calculate the impedance of the circuit.
solution_steps: Calculate inductive reactance: X_L = 2pi f L = 2 \times 3.1416 \times 50 \times 0.5 = 157.08 Omega.
Calculate capacitive reactance: X_C = 1 / (2pi f C) = 1 / (2 \times 3.1416 \times 50 \times 10 \times 10^{-6}) = 318.31 Omega.
Calculate impedance using Z = sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}.

solved_numericals.question: Find the resonant frequency and the Q-factor of a series LCR circuit containing an inductor of 2 H, a capacitor of 32 mu F, and a resistance of 10 Omega.
solution_steps: Calculate resonant frequency: f_0 = 1 / (2pi sqrt{LC}) = 1 / (2 \times 3.1416 \times sqrt{2 \times 32 \times 10^{-6}}).
Calculate angular resonant frequency: omega_0 = 2pi f_0 = 2 \times 3.1416 \times 19.89 approx 125 rad/s.
Calculate Q-factor: Q = omega_0 L / R = (125 \times 2) / 10 = 25.

solved_numericals.question: A series LCR circuit has R = 20 Omega, L = 0.4 H, and C = 100 mu F. Determine the bandwidth of the resonance curve.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for bandwidth in a series LCR circuit: Deltaomega = R / L.
Substitute the given values: R = 20 Omega and L = 0.4 H.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes ideal lumped circuit elements where resistance, inductance, and capacitance are localized and independent of frequency (skin effect and dielectric losses are neglected).

common_misconceptions.wrong: At resonance, the voltage across the inductor and capacitor individually is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: At resonance, the net reactive voltage (V_L - V_C) is zero, but individual voltages V_L and V_C can be very high and equal in magnitude.
common_misconceptions.why: Individual reactances cancel each other out in series due to opposite phase angles, but finite current still produces potential drops across L and C.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit depends on the resistance R.
common_misconceptions.correct: The resonant frequency depends only on inductance L and capacitance C (omega_0 = 1/sqrt{LC}).
common_misconceptions.why: Resistance only affects the damping and the sharpness of the resonance curve (bandwidth), not the frequency at which X_L = X_C.

quick_revision: At series resonance, X_L = X_C, impedance is minimum (Z = R), current is maximum, and power factor is unity.
Inductive Reactance: X_L = omega L = 2pi f L
Capacitive Reactance: X_C = \frac{1}{omega C} = \frac{1}{2pi f C}
